sections.target: past simple: regular and irregular verbs
sections.explanation: Use the past simple for a finished action at a finished time. Regular verbs take -ed: walked, asked, cooked. Irregular verbs change shape instead, and you learn them one by one: go becomes went, buy becomes bought, take becomes took. There is no rule that predicts them, so the only way is to meet them often and use them.
sections.when_to_use: When the action is over and the time it happened in is over too.
sections.when_not_to: Not when the time is still open, like today or this week.
examples: I walked home because the bus never came.
She bought the wrong milk again yesterday.
We took the late train and got soaked.

mistake.said: I buyed a coat in the sale.
mistake.corrected: I bought a coat in the sale.
mistake.why: Buy is irregular, so it doesn't take -ed.

sections.target: past continuous for what was going on around it
sections.explanation: The past continuous sets the scene. It describes something already in progress, stretching across a moment rather than finishing at it. Build it with was or were plus the -ing form: I was cooking, they were waiting. You reach for it when you want the background of a story rather than the events themselves.
sections.when_to_use: When you want the background, the thing already happening around the moment.
sections.when_not_to: Not for a quick finished action, and not for states like know or want.
examples: I was cooking when the smoke alarm went off.
They were waiting outside in the rain.
The neighbours were arguing again at midnight.

mistake.said: I was knowing the answer straight away.
mistake.corrected: I knew the answer straight away.
mistake.why: Know is a state, so it doesn't take the -ing form.

sections.target: past simple and past continuous in the same sentence
sections.explanation: Put the two together and you get a story. The past continuous is the longer background, and the past simple is the shorter thing that cuts into it. Join them with when or while: while I was walking home, it started to rain. The interrupting action almost always takes the past simple.
sections.when_to_use: When a short event lands in the middle of something longer.
sections.when_not_to: Not when both actions simply followed each other in order.
examples: While I was walking home, it started to rain.
He was sleeping when his phone rang.
We were eating when the lights went out.

mistake.said: While I walked home, it was starting to rain.
mistake.corrected: While I was walking home, it started to rain.
mistake.why: The longer background takes the continuous, not the short event.

sections.target: time linkers: then, after that, a bit later
sections.explanation: Linkers hold a story together and stop it sounding like a list. Then moves you straight on to the next thing. After that does the same but feels a little slower. A bit later leaves a gap you don't have to explain. Drop them in at the front of a sentence and the order becomes obvious.
sections.when_to_use: When you're telling somebody several things that happened in order.
sections.when_not_to: Not in every sentence, or the story starts to sound like a list.
examples: We had a coffee, then we walked to the park.
After that, the rain got much worse.
A bit later, she called to apologise.

mistake.said: We had a coffee. Then. We walked to the park.
mistake.corrected: We had a coffee, then we walked to the park.
mistake.why: Then joins the two halves, so it can't stand alone.
